name: Samaritanism
areas: the Samaritans' holy place, which they hold to be the Israelites' original sanctuary; the Gerizim temple was destroyed around 120 BCE
the Samaritan community of Holon, Israel, has its own local priest
marks: The temple here, built in the 5th century BCE, was destroyed by John Hyrcanus around 120 BCE; Samaritans revere the mountain as God's holy place.
The High Priest lives on Mount Gerizim; since 1624 the oldest member of the priestly family has been chosen for the office.
The Samaritan community of Holon, Israel, has its own local priest.
notes: John Hyrcanus destroys the temple on Mount Gerizim and brings Samaria under his control (around 120 BCE); mutual hostility between Jews and Samaritans lasts, and each comes to see the Samaritan faith as distinct from Judaism.
By the time of Jesus, Samaritans and Jews deeply disparage one another, as the Parable of the Good Samaritan shows.
The Byzantine Empire persecutes the Samaritans, practically annihilating them after their revolts of the 5th and 6th centuries.
Samaritan texts take shape: the legendary Aramaic Al-Asatir (11th and 12th centuries) and the halakhic Kitab at-Tabbah (12th century).
Abu'l-Fath writes a major work of Samaritan history in the 14th century, as does Yosef Al Ascar the halakhic Kitab al-Kafi.
Since 1624 the oldest member of the priestly family is chosen as High Priest, who lives on Mount Gerizim.
The priestly family is 28 percent of the community in 2003; as of 2025 there are approximately 900 registered communal Samaritans.
